title: Miller's youth, first bands, piano teachers, Earl Foster and New Orleans pianists
summary: Bill Russell opens the 1964 interview. Miller gives his birth and nickname, his piccolo-playing father, learning ukulele, organ and piano by ear, first jobs from 1927, and sixteen years with Earl Foster. He also recalls other New Orleans pianists, house parties and police raids.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: The End This is an interview with Mr. Singh Miller. This is Bill Russell doing the interviewing. And the date is about the tenth of... Is this the eleventh? Lost track of the date. The eleventh of December, 1964. We're recording this down at 732 St. Peter Street. What is your full name? My name is James Edward Miller. James Edward Miller. Everyone calls me Singh. How did you get that nickname? I've been singing since I was a little bit of a boy. Actually, from your singing? From school days. Now, where were you born? Born in New Orleans. Right here in New Orleans. What part of town? I was born in the Twelfth Ward. In the Twelfth Ward. Let's see, is that the... On Gentile Street, Gentile Annunciation. Downtown then? Uptown. Oh, Annunciation. My daddy was a musician. My daddy used to be a piccolo player. I used to listen to him play all the time when I was a boy. And I said, I hope that when I grow up I'll learn how to play some type of music. But when I started playing music, I had a violin like you did, but I made a ukulele out of my violin. Oh, and I just picked it then. And started picking it. So I started up with some boys, four fellas, they're still living. Eddie Hickman, Julius Simpson, and a saxophone player, he's dead now. Can't call his name no more now. Did you get the date when you were born? June 17, 1913. 1913. And about how old were you then when you first played in that time? Well, I first started music. I started around 1920. My first job playing I was around 1927. Playing music around 1927. I played at the O.K. Lounge. We used to play two nights a week, Friday and Saturday, Cutler's Giant. What was that about? On Tulane? No, it was on the South Street. Oh, on the South. On the South Street. Then I started going from joint to joint. I met Kit Howard. I got in his band. I started playing with him. I played with Henry Russ. He brought me a long ways. Father Al helped me a long ways. I played the banjo for a while. I used to go try to play the banjo. And Father Al, in his place. I still could play the banjo, still have my banjo. And from time and time, even with Papa John, the bass player down there, I got on his bass and learned to play the bass a little bit. I learned to play the bass. I still play the bass now, but that's make my fingers look sore. If I play on every night, it wouldn't be sore. But playing once in a while, I get my fingers sore. And I play the South Street on now. Well. My first big band I played was with J. Mike Shane. Oh, yes. The fellow from Kansas City? Yes. Oh, yeah. I heard that band years ago, 1938 or so. Yeah. We used to play down in the world. I used to go from different states with him. Then I played with the James Brothers from Homer. Oh, out west. Yeah. In Louisiana. Yeah. Anybody else in that band from New Orleans that we might know of? Well, with the drummer, he was named Claiborne Williams. Oh. Was it the son of the old man, Claiborne Williams? It was the son. It was the son of him. In other words, they called him Crip. Yeah. Crip. But during the time I learned how to get on to play the piano. Yeah. When did you start on piano? Did you? Well, I started piano in... I started actually on piano in 1928. I actually started on the piano. In fact, I started on the organ. Oh, the little reed organ. Yeah. At school. Yeah. The teachers used to call me up and after recess, I'd be, instead of going on the outside, going in and banging on the organ. By the way, where did you go to school? I went to the Lutheran. I went to J.W. Hoppin. I went to the phone. But you're all here in the... Oh, no. ...in New Orleans. Mm-hmm. And... Did you have any lessons on piano or pick it up or...? No one had never showed me a note on the piano. No, everything I knew, even around guys learning how to read notes. Yeah. I just picked up from experience. My daddy died when I was five. Well, you never did know him so awfully well then. Well, I still remember his face. You remember him well? I remember his face. In other words, my brother's a picture of him. Really? My brother's a picture of my dad. Mm-hmm. But my brother, he couldn't even whistle. He doesn't go into music. He couldn't whistle. He couldn't whistle. Is he older than you or younger? He's older now. He's a year and nine months old now. But my sister could play. My sister, I'm nine years older than my sister, well she started playing after, I started playing the piano. And she used to watch me play the keys. And she took a piano then too? Yeah, she took a piano. Yeah. But so far as me ever learning how to read music, what I learned how to read, I learned to read being all guys. Yeah. Did you have the piano in your home? Never had a piano in my life. Never had a piano in my life. Never had a piano in my life. Never, every time I had a band practice, I would practice at somebody's house, about a few hours a night like that. And I worked with Earl Foster, I worked with him about sixteen years. One man, sixteen years. Just here, I'm working with him, I'm in the county of Zill right now, he's triple right now. But I started off with him when they had four pieces at the Carnival Club on Drive Street, Drive and U-Turk, they had a joint called the Carnival Club. And it was Joe Battley. Joe? Joe Battley, trumpet player. Battley. Battley. Battley, Battley. Battley. Battley. I don't know him. He's a youngster, isn't he? Is he still around? Yeah, he's still around. He's a good trumpet player too. Yeah. In fact, him and I, now that's who actually taught me, him and his boy Cliff Bruce, let me now read a little bit. Joe Battley and Cliff Bruce. Of course, Cliff Bruce, he doesn't play that anymore. You know, like I told you, he passed. You see? But those are the two guys that brought me into music life, into the world. Who was the leader of that band, the Dryads? Earl Foster. Who? Earl Foster. Earl Foster. Oh, yes. Earl Foster, yes. In other words, I played six years straight with him in Buggalos at the Club Plantation. And I worked behind a much more piano player than what I was, but everybody liked my playing better than they did his. He had a good style, I guess, that people liked. He had a better style than he did. Now, in other words, I used to go back to Bazzari's school. That's all I would call him Richard. I never knew his last name. I was going to ask about some of the other piano players when you were even a little kid before you did that. Well, I always did know Mrs. Kimball. Oh, yes. I knew her before she got married to Mr. Kimball. Yes. And now Miss Dolly, I knew her boys but I didn't know her. Yeah. I guess you heard Walter Pijon. Walter Pijon and I, we played a duet just like you did on the day tonight. Oh, yeah. We played a duet at the Opsin House. Now, I remember Fat Pijon when Pijon was playing on the boat, on the steam of the girls there. Yeah. With Faith Marvin there. Well. He was about to remember when they had all that going on at that time. Now, Fat Pijon used to play with Papa Celestine. Many people don't know that, but I know that. I don't remember that. Yeah. He played with Papa Celestine. In other words, he was playing piano with Papa Celestine. Yeah. Not Miss Kim. Fat Pijon was playing. I'm still trying to call this guy his piano player. Stack Lee. Oh, yeah. Stack Lee. Yeah. Stack Lee. Those are the kind of piano players that I came up with. Steve Lewis Stack Lee, Big Eye Lewis, and one more was Toots. His name is Isidore. Isidore Washington is his name. Isidore Washington. But everybody calls him Toots. Toots. Toots. Where did he work? He didn't ever work. Just played around any joint you could have. Any joint he wanted to be around. Yeah. Toots was playing before I got married. I was married in 1932. And Toots was still playing then. Yeah. Did he play house parties and all that? We used to play house parties. Toots would play in one block and I would play the next block. Yeah. House parties. But most people would be at my party. Yeah. You know during that time people would have fish fires and had the red lights on the gate. Yeah. I've heard about that. Well some of them didn't have none. Some of them did have. In other words during that time they used to sell moonshine liquor during that time. You know. Yeah. They sell that old moonshine liquor. So much of a Coca Cola bottle full of whatever kind of bottle they might put it in. It's settled so much.
